cues.text: Chapter four is titled Smart factories, analytics and operational decisions.
We start with a question every plant manager faces: how do you keep machines running without wasting money on unnecessary repairs, and without being caught out by a sudden breakdown?
Predictive maintenance estimates the risk that an asset will fail.
It draws on three inputs: sensor data, maintenance history and operating context.
Operating context means things like load, temperature, running hours and the conditions the machine works in.
To see what is distinctive about predictive maintenance, compare it with three other approaches.
Preventive maintenance follows a schedule, so you service a machine at fixed intervals whether or not it needs it.
Corrective maintenance repairs the machine after it has failed.
Condition-based maintenance acts on the observed condition of the asset.
If a reading crosses a threshold, you act.
Predictive maintenance goes one step further and forecasts the likely future need for maintenance.
The difference is timing.
Preventive follows the calendar, corrective follows the failure, condition-based follows the current state, and predictive follows a forecast.
None of these is always best.
You choose according to four things: how critical the asset is, its failure modes, the quality of your data, and the costs involved.
A minor asset that is cheap to replace may not justify a predictive model.
A critical machine whose failure stops the whole line may justify one, provided you have data good enough to support it.
Now consider an example.
A Nigerian manufacturing plant monitors the vibration and temperature of its motors.
This is an illustrative example of how the pieces fit together.
It is not evidence of a measured result.
The sensors send their data to an edge gateway.
An edge gateway sits close to the machines, so data can be processed locally rather than only far away.
A validated model identifies abnormal trends in that data.
When it does, local alarms notify operators and create maintenance requests, so the response begins at the plant.
The cloud then analyses patterns across many assets and helps improve planning.
So the local layer handles the fast response, and the cloud handles the wider learning.
One more element matters here.
A separate engineered safety system protects workers and machinery.
Experimental AI should not override validated safety limits.
The analytics improves maintenance decisions, but worker and machine protection stays with the validated safety system.
Next, what makes a factory smart?
The source lists these capabilities: real-time monitoring, automated quality inspection, adaptive production, resource optimisation, traceability and connected logistics.
Real-time monitoring shows what is happening on the line as it happens.
Automated quality inspection checks products automatically.
Adaptive production adjusts to conditions.
Resource optimisation makes better use of inputs.
Traceability lets you follow products and materials through the process.
Connected logistics links the movement of goods into the same picture.
Mass customisation uses flexible production to tailor products efficiently.
The aim is to give customers products fitted to them without losing the efficiency of organised production.
Additive manufacturing, which is often called 3D printing, can support prototypes or low-volume parts.
But material quality, speed and certification matter.
It is not automatically the right choice for every part.
To judge how well equipment is being used, we use a metric called overall equipment effectiveness, or OEE.
The formula is OEE equals availability times performance times quality.
Take the source example, with availability of 90 percent, performance of 95 percent and quality of 98 percent.
Then OEE equals 0.90 times 0.95 times 0.98.
First, 0.90 times 0.95 gives 0.855.
Then 0.855 times 0.98 gives 0.8379.
So OEE is 83.79 percent.
Each part has a specific meaning.
Availability accounts for planned production time and downtime.
Performance compares the actual output rate with the ideal rate.
Quality measures good output against total output.
Because the three are multiplied, a weakness in any one of them pulls the whole figure down.
You must also define boundaries consistently.
If one team counts a stoppage as downtime and another does not, the numbers cannot be compared.
Now a worked downtime example.
A line loses 10 hours a month, and monitoring reduces that to 6 hours.
The reduction is 10 minus 6, divided by 10.
That is 4 divided by 10, which is 40 percent.
Suppose each hour of lost production costs ₦200,000 in lost contribution.
Then the 4 hours avoided give ₦800,000 in gross avoided loss each month.
Note the word gross.
That figure comes before implementation and maintenance costs.
And be careful not to treat every avoided downtime hour as realised revenue.
If demand or other constraints limit production, the extra running time may not turn into extra sales.
Finally, these ideas reach well beyond manufacturing.
The source gives five areas.
In agriculture, applications include soil and moisture monitoring, precision irrigation and equipment tracking.
In healthcare, there is remote patient monitoring, with clinical escalation and privacy controls.
Escalation means a clinician responds when readings call for it, and privacy controls protect patient data.
In logistics, applications include GPS, cold-chain temperature monitoring and asset tracking.
The cold chain is the temperature-controlled path of goods that must stay cool.
In energy, there are smart meters, demand management and grid monitoring.
And in smart cities, applications include traffic, lighting, waste collection and emergency coordination.
In every one of these settings the pattern is the same as in the factory.
Sensors collect data, analytics interprets it, and people or systems act on it.
The value comes from the operational decision at the end.
